name: Femi Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an office administrator at a housing association, so we look after about two thousand rented homes. I sit on the repairs desk with three others, booking plumbers and electricians into tenants' homes, filing the job sheets and chasing the paperwork when a contractor forgets to send it. I've been there just under two years and I'm still the slow one, honestly. I keep a paper diary next to the screen because the booking system freezes and I don't trust it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tenants, mostly. There's an old man called Mr Okafor who rings every Tuesday about his boiler, and I know his whole life story now. What wears me out is the system, and the targets on how fast we close a job. My manager Dennis keeps saying I should use the shortcuts, but I'd rather get it right than get it fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at work was going on about AI like it was going to run the place, and it turns out it just writes a slightly better email. I'd probably say it in the union group chat, because Carol, our rep, has been warning people not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be a bit worried, because even the small stuff it automates is my stuff. The bit it saves time on is booking and filing, and that's most of my day. If they save half an hour per person, somebody upstairs will work out that four people on the desk could be three. And I'm the newest and the slowest, so I know which chair goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, but I'd ask Carol to make sure any new tools come with proper training and no job cuts. I'd keep putting a hundred a month into savings like I do now. Ruth, my partner, and I want to move out of the flat above the chip shop next year, so I wouldn't change that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not fully relaxed. AI fizzling out is like a storm missing the house when the roof was already leaking. The rent's still going up and the association's budget still gets cut every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the roof was already leaking. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our funding gets squeezed every year, and they froze two posts last spring. Nobody got sacked, but when Joanne left they didn't replace her, and we just took on her tenants. So even with AI doing nothing much, I'm not going to call myself safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they did try to cut one person on the desk, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Carol and get my name down for any meeting. I'm not a fighter by nature, but I'd rather stand with the others than sit quietly and hope it's someone else. I'd also update my CV that weekend, which I haven't touched since I got this job.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be **mostly hype**, a slightly better email tool.
I'd back our **union rep** and tell people not to panic.
think: Even the small automation hits **booking and filing**, which is most of my day.
If the desk shrinks from four to three, I'm the **newest and slowest**.
do: Ask the **union** to make sure new tools come with training and no cuts.
Keep saving **£100 a month** and stick with the plan to move next year.
feel: **Relieved** the big change didn't come, but not relaxed.
Still **worried** about rent rises and yearly budget cuts.
S0.quote: AI fizzling out is like a storm missing the house when the roof was already leaking.
fieldNote: He hears **routine automation** as aimed at his exact tasks, not at the office in general.
The real pressure is **budget cuts** and unfilled posts, which existed long before AI.
He calls himself **not a fighter** but turns to the union first, before anything else.

steps.text: Keep the paper diary and do the repairs bookings as now
Ask the union rep to get a no-cuts promise on new tools
Keep putting 100 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is being done to us, not with us. I'd say the housing association should be spending money on fixing damp, not on a chatbot. I'd probably post that on Facebook too, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes. Booking, checking job sheets and answering tenants are literally the list on that card. They'd put in a tenant app that books the plumber straight into the diary, and the desk goes from four people to maybe one supervisor and the app. Dennis would keep Priya because she's quick and does the reports, and I'd be out within two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every meeting Carol calls and push for a deal where anyone who goes gets retrained or moved, not just shown the door. I'd ask Dennis straight out whether there's a caretaker or estates job going, because walking round the blocks is still a person's job for now. I'd stop the extra spending, like the takeaways on Fridays, and try to get the savings from three months to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. I never got on with computers. I'm 27 and I already feel behind, and now the computer's going to do my job better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try learning the new tools, to stay on the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the training if it was in work time, because I'd be stupid not to. But I'm not going to pretend I'd be the one running it. Priya picks up these things in an afternoon, and it takes me a fortnight, and they'd both see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth the night you found out the desk was shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm probably going, and that I'd rather go into estates and get my hands dirty than fight for a chair I'm going to lose anyway. Her bus job's safe for a good while yet, so we wouldn't starve. But the move out of the flat would have to wait, and she'd be gutted about that.

say: I'd say the change is being **done to us**, not with us.
The association should spend on **fixing damp**, not on a chatbot.
think: Booking, checking and answering tenants is **my whole job**, and an app could do it.
I expect to be **out within two years**, with the quick colleague kept on.
do: Join every **union meeting** and push for retraining or redeployment for anyone cut.
Ask about a **caretaker or estates** job and stop the Friday takeaways.
feel: **Sick** and behind, at 27, with a computer about to beat him.
Some **comfort** that his partner's bus job is safe for now.
S1.quote: I'm 27 and I already feel behind, and now the computer's going to do my job better than me.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** outright, not just change it, and names who stays.
His instinct is to move to **hands-on estates work** rather than compete on the screen.
Partner Ruth's bus job is the **household's anchor**, which keeps this short of panic.

steps.text: Push the union for retraining or redeployment for anyone cut from the desk
Ask Dennis about caretaker or estates jobs on the blocks
Stop Friday takeaways and build savings from three months to five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. You can't let a few tech firms switch off half the jobs in the country in two years. I'd be at the march, I'd sign every petition, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be finished in office work by 2028, and I'm not sure I'd find my feet. I've only got a school certificate and two years of booking plumbers. The robots coming three years later means the estates job would buy me time, but only till 2031. Ruth's bus would be driving itself about then too, so it's both of us, one after the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd beg Dennis for anything on the estates team, cleaning bins, changing bulbs, whatever. I'd cut every bit of spending, cancel the gym and the streaming, and put the move off for good. I'd sign up with the union for whatever they're fighting for, a wage from the government or a slower roll-out. Beyond that I honestly don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd be lying awake doing sums with no answer at the bottom. Two years isn't long enough for someone like me to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what you'd do after that. Is there anything that would help you think it through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody sitting me down and telling me what's actually still going to need people. Not a website, a person. My dad's a mechanic, and he'd say learn a trade, but a trade is three or four years and the robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings would go on rent first, so three months, maybe four if we're careful. Then I'd be asking my mum if we could move back in with her, which at 27 with my girlfriend is not something I want to picture. Ruth would hate it, and so would I.

say: The **government** has to step in before tech firms switch off half the jobs.
I'd be at the **march** and sign every petition going.
think: My **office work** would be finished by 2028, with only a school certificate behind me.
An estates job buys **time till 2031**, when Ruth's bus also drives itself.
do: Beg for **any estates work**, from cleaning bins to changing bulbs.
Cancel the **gym and streaming**, and put the move off for good.
Back whatever the union fights for, like a **government wage**.
feel: Like the **floor's gone**, lying awake doing sums with no answer.
**Hopeless** that two years is enough for him to become someone else.
S2.quote: Two years isn't long enough for someone like me to become someone else.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** past the first month and says so plainly.
The **robot gap** of three years feels too short to learn a trade.
Both household jobs fall **one after the other**, so nothing is left to lean on except his mother.

steps.text: Ask Dennis for any estates job, even cleaning bins or changing bulbs
Cancel the gym and streaming and stop all extras
Join union marches for a government wage or slower roll-out
Ask his mum about moving back in with Ruth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: the government needs rules and needs them now, while there's still time. I'd say five years is a warning, so there's no excuse this time. I'd want the union pushing for a shorter week, so the work left gets shared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me a shot at something with my hands, but only just. If AGI lands in 2031 and the robots in 2034, a trade I start in 2027 would give me four or five years of proper earning. My dad says plumbers will always be needed, and I've booked enough of them to know what they earn. The desk job I'd lose around 2030, I reckon, before it even arrives properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening plumbing course at the college, two nights a week. I'd ask the association whether their maintenance contractor takes apprentices, because I know the boss there from the phone. I'd keep the desk job as long as it lasts and save every bit of overtime. Ruth and I would still move, but to somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but there's a door in it, at least. With the fast one there's no door. Here there's a door and I'd have to go through it, which isn't me, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've told me you avoid change. What would make you actually sign up for that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the desk shrink with my own eyes. If Joanne's chair stays empty and then Priya's goes, I'd know. I'm slow to move, but I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, our rep, honestly. She's 58 and she's been at the association 30 years, and she's got nowhere to go. I'd be scared for me, but I've got time to be scared in. She hasn't.

say: Five years is a **warning**, so there's no excuse for having no rules.
The union should push for a **shorter week** to share the work left.
think: Five years gives me a shot at **plumbing**, with a few years of earning before robots.
I expect to lose the **desk job around 2030**, before AGI properly lands.
do: Start an **evening plumbing** course at the college, two nights a week.
Ask the **maintenance contractor** about an apprenticeship.
Save all **overtime** and move somewhere cheaper with Ruth.
feel: **Scared**, but this time there's a door to walk through.
**Worried** for older colleagues who have no time to change.
S3.quote: With the fast one there's no door. Here there's a door and I'd have to go through it, which isn't me, but I'd do it.
fieldNote: The **five-year warning** turns despair into a reluctant plan to retrain in plumbing.
He still expects to **lose the desk job**, just with some time to act.
His concern shifts to his **older union rep**, who has no time to change.

steps.text: Sign up for an evening plumbing course at the college
Ask the maintenance contractor about taking him on as an apprentice
Bank every bit of overtime from the desk job
Move with Ruth to a cheaper flat instead of a nicer one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so let's do it properly. Retraining paid for by the government, not by people like me out of their own pocket. I'd say it in the union meetings, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years takes the panic out of it for me. I'd still lose the desk job, probably years before 2036, because the tools would creep in before the big day. But I could train in plumbing, get qualified, and have eight or nine years on the tools before the robots arrive around 2039. By then I'd be 40, and that's a problem for 40-year-old me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait a year or two and see if it's real, because that's what I'm like. Then I'd start the plumbing course and ask about an apprenticeship. I'd keep saving the hundred a month, and Ruth and I would get the flat we want, maybe even think about a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more like normal nervous. It's the kind of worry everyone has about their job, not the lying-awake kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the association starts losing desk staff and not replacing them. And whether the contractors start booking themselves in through some app instead of ringing me. If the old man who rings me every Tuesday about his boiler starts getting a machine instead, that's my sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if you waited too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be the guy at 33 doing a course with 17-year-olds. I'd do it anyway. My dad retrained at 35 when the factory shut, and he never complained about it once.

say: Ten years is enough to do **retraining properly**, paid for by the government.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to fund it.
think: I'd still lose the **desk job** well before 2036, as tools creep in.
Plumbing would give me **eight or nine years** on the tools before robots arrive.
do: Wait **a year or two** to see whether the desk really shrinks.
Then start a **plumbing course** and look for an apprenticeship.
Keep saving **£100 a month** and look at a flat deposit with Ruth.
feel: **Normal nervous**, like anyone about their job, not the lying-awake kind.
S4.quote: If the old man who rings me every Tuesday about his boiler starts getting a machine instead, that's my sign.
fieldNote: He would **wait and watch** first, true to his cautious nature, then switch to a trade.
His warning sign is a **regular tenant's call** going to a machine, not a news story.
His father **retraining at 35** after a factory closed is his model for coping.

steps.text: Watch for a year whether desk staff are not replaced
Start a plumbing course and look for an apprenticeship
Vote for whoever funds retraining for office workers
Keep saving 100 a month toward a flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years, no plan, and both of us losing our jobs one after the other. What would help is someone paying for a trade course and paying me a wage while I do it, so I'm not choosing between rent and retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. If a machine answers the repairs line, who notices that Mr Okafor sounds confused this week, or that a family's been living with black mould for months? I'm not quick at my job, but I notice people, and I don't think a computer gets told the things they tell me.

headlineQuote: I'm not quick at my job, but I notice people, and I don't think a computer gets told the things they tell me.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** repairs-desk administrator at a housing association, still the slowest on a team of four.
He keeps a **paper diary**, never uses AI tools, and leans on the union and his partner's bus job.
He moves from **uneasy** about budget cuts to **panicked** when AGI arrives in two years.
With five or ten years' warning he plans to **retrain as a plumber**, reluctantly but firmly.
He blames **tech firms and government** inaction, and values the human side of dealing with tenants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no plan and both household jobs falling one after the other.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid trade course** with a wage during training, so he isn't choosing between rent and retraining.
